theorem injOn (h : LeftInvOn f₁' f s) : InjOn f s := fun x₁ h₁ x₂ h₂ heq =>
  calc
    x₁ = f₁' (f x₁) := Eq.symm <| h h₁
    _ = f₁' (f x₂) := congr_arg f₁' heq
    _ = x₂ := h h₂

def hasDecEq : (φ ψ : Formula α) → Decidable (φ = ψ)
  | ⊥, ψ => by
    cases ψ using cases' <;>
    { simp; try { exact isFalse not_false }; try { exact isTrue trivial } }
  | ⊤, ψ => by
    cases ψ using cases' <;>
    { simp; try { exact isFalse not_false }; try { exact isTrue trivial } }
  | atom a, ψ => by
    cases ψ using cases' <;> try { simp; exact isFalse not_false }
    simp; exact decEq _ _
  | ∼φ, ψ => by
    cases ψ using cases' <;> try { simp; exact isFalse not_false }
    case hneg φ' =>
      exact match hasDecEq φ φ' with
      | isTrue hp  => isTrue (by simp[hp])
      | isFalse hp => isFalse (by simp[hp])
  | φ ➝ ψ, χ => by
    cases χ using cases' <;> try { simp; exact isFalse not_false }
    case himp φ' ψ' =>
      exact match hasDecEq φ φ' with
      | isTrue hp =>
        match hasDecEq ψ ψ' with
        | isTrue hq  => isTrue (hp ▸ hq ▸ rfl)
        | isFalse hq => isFalse (by simp[hp, hq])
      | isFalse hp => isFalse (by simp[hp])
  | φ ⋏ ψ, χ => by
    cases χ using cases' <;> try { simp; exact isFalse not_false }
    case hand φ' ψ' =>
      exact match hasDecEq φ φ' with
      | isTrue hp =>
        match hasDecEq ψ ψ' with
        | isTrue hq  => isTrue (hp ▸ hq ▸ rfl)
        | isFalse hq => isFalse (by simp[hp, hq])
      | isFalse hp => isFalse (by simp[hp])
  | φ ⋎ ψ, χ => by
    cases χ using cases' <;> try { simp; exact isFalse not_false }
    case hor φ' ψ' =>
      exact match hasDecEq φ φ' with
      | isTrue hp =>
        match hasDecEq ψ ψ' with
        | isTrue hq  => isTrue (hp ▸ hq ▸ rfl)
        | isFalse hq => isFalse (by simp[hp, hq])
      | isFalse hp => isFalse (by simp[hp])

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : Repr (Formula α) := ⟨fun t _ => toStr t⟩
instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

end ToString

@[simp] lemma and_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋏ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋏ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Wedge.wedge]
@[simp] lemma or_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋎ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋎ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Vee.vee]
@[simp] lemma imp_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ➝ φ₂ = ψ₁ ➝ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Arrow.arrow]
@[simp] lemma neg_inj (φ ψ : Formula α) : ∼φ = ∼ψ ↔ φ = ψ := by simp[Tilde.tilde]

-- lemma neg_def (φ : Formula α) : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥ := rfl

lemma iff_def (φ ψ : Formula α) : φ ⭤ ψ = (φ ➝ ψ) ⋏ (ψ ➝ φ) := by rfl

def complexity : Formula α → ℕ
| atom _  => 0
| ⊤       => 0
| ⊥       => 0
| ∼φ      => φ.complexity + 1
| φ ➝ ψ  => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋏ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋎ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1

@[simp] lemma complexity_bot : complexity (⊥ : Formula α) = 0 := rfl
@[simp] lemma complexity_top : complexity (⊤ : Formula α) = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma complexity_atom (a : α) : complexity (atom a) = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma complexity_imp (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (φ ➝ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl
@[simp] lemma complexity_imp' (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (imp φ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma complexity_and (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (φ ⋏ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl
@[simp] lemma complexity_and' (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (and φ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma complexity_or (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (φ ⋎ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl
@[simp] lemma complexity_or' (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (or φ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl

@[elab_as_elim]
def cases' {C : Formula α → Sort w}
    (hfalsum : C ⊥)
    (hverum  : C ⊤)
    (hatom   : ∀ a : α, C (atom a))
    (hneg    : ∀ φ : Formula α, C (∼φ))
    (himp    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ➝ ψ))
    (hand    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ⋏ ψ))
    (hor     : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ⋎ ψ))
    : (φ : Formula α) → C φ
  | ⊥       => hfalsum
  | ⊤       => hverum
  | atom a  => hatom a
  | ∼φ      => hneg φ
  | φ ➝ ψ  => himp φ ψ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => hand φ ψ
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => hor φ ψ

@[elab_as_elim]
def rec' {C : Formula α → Sort w}
  (hfalsum : C ⊥)
  (hverum  : C ⊤)
  (hatom   : ∀ a : α, C (atom a))
  (hneg    : ∀ φ : Formula α, C φ → C (∼φ))
  (himp    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C φ → C ψ → C (φ ➝ ψ))
  (hand    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C φ → C ψ → C (φ ⋏ ψ))
  (hor     : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C φ → C ψ → C (φ ⋎ ψ))
  : (φ : Formula α) → C φ
  | ⊥       => hfalsum
  | ⊤       => hverum
  | atom a  => hatom a
  | ∼φ      => hneg φ (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor φ)
  | φ ➝ ψ  => himp φ ψ (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor φ) (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor ψ)
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => hand φ ψ (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor φ) (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor ψ)
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => hor φ ψ (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor φ) (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor ψ)

section Decidable

variable [DecidableEq α]

def hasDecEq : (φ ψ : Formula α) → Decidable (φ = ψ)
  | ⊥, ψ => by
    exact?

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C0_dependencies.content:
def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : Repr (Formula α) := ⟨fun t _ => toStr t⟩
instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

end ToString

@[simp] lemma and_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋏ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋏ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Wedge.wedge]
@[simp] lemma or_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋎ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋎ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Vee.vee]
@[simp] lemma imp_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ➝ φ₂ = ψ₁ ➝ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Arrow.arrow]
@[simp] lemma neg_inj (φ ψ : Formula α) : ∼φ = ∼ψ ↔ φ = ψ := by simp[Tilde.tilde]

-- lemma neg_def (φ : Formula α) : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥ := rfl

lemma iff_def (φ ψ : Formula α) : φ ⭤ ψ = (φ ➝ ψ) ⋏ (ψ ➝ φ) := by rfl

def complexity : Formula α → ℕ
| atom _  => 0
| ⊤       => 0
| ⊥       => 0
| ∼φ      => φ.complexity + 1
| φ ➝ ψ  => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋏ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋎ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

informal_statement: Substituting any term into the false formula $\bot$ results in $\bot$ itself.
informal_proof: By definition, substituting any term into the formula $\bot$ does not alter its truth value. The false formula $\bot$ remains false regardless of the substitution applied, so substituting into $\bot$ results in $\bot$.

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : Repr (Formula α) := ⟨fun t _ => toStr t⟩
instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

end ToString

@[simp] lemma and_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋏ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋏ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Wedge.wedge]
@[simp] lemma or_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋎ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋎ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Vee.vee]
@[simp] lemma imp_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ➝ φ₂ = ψ₁ ➝ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Arrow.arrow]
@[simp] lemma neg_inj (φ ψ : Formula α) : ∼φ = ∼ψ ↔ φ = ψ := by simp[Tilde.tilde]

-- lemma neg_def (φ : Formula α) : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥ := rfl

lemma iff_def (φ ψ : Formula α) : φ ⭤ ψ = (φ ➝ ψ) ⋏ (ψ ➝ φ) := by rfl

def complexity : Formula α → ℕ
| atom _  => 0
| ⊤       => 0
| ⊥       => 0
| ∼φ      => φ.complexity + 1
| φ ➝ ψ  => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋏ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋎ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1

@[simp] lemma complexity_bot : complexity (⊥ : Formula α) = 0 := rfl
@[simp] lemma complexity_top : complexity (⊤ : Formula α) = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma complexity_atom (a : α) : complexity (atom a) = 0 := rfl

@[simp] lemma complexity_imp (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (φ ➝ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl
@[simp] lemma complexity_imp' (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (imp φ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma complexity_and (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (φ ⋏ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl
@[simp] lemma complexity_and' (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (and φ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl

@[simp] lemma complexity_or (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (φ ⋎ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl
@[simp] lemma complexity_or' (φ ψ : Formula α) : complexity (or φ ψ) = max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1 := rfl

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: For every natural number \( n \), there exists a prime number \( p \) such that \( p \) is greater than \( n \). Equivalently, there are infinitely many prime numbers.
informal_proof:
First, let’s consider an arbitrary natural number \( n \). We wish to show that there exists a prime number \( p \) such that \( p > n \). To do this, consider the number \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), where \( ! \) denotes the factorial operation.

The factorial \( (n + 1)! \) is the product of all positive integers up to \( n + 1 \). Therefore, \( (n + 1)! \) is greater than or equal to \( 2 \), and so \( (n + 1)! + 1 \) is at least \( 3 \).

Now, by the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, every integer greater than 1 has at least one prime factor. Let \( p \) be a prime factor of \( (n + 1)! + 1 \). We assert that \( p \) must be greater than \( n \).

Assume, for contradiction, that \( p \leq n \). Since \( p \) is a prime factor of \( (n + 1)! \), it divides \( (n + 1)! \). Additionally, by definition, \( p \) divides \( (n + 1)! + 1 \). Therefore, \( p \) divides the difference between these two numbers:

\[
((n + 1)! + 1) - (n + 1)! = 1
\]

This implies that \( p \) divides \( 1 \). However, the only positive integer that divides \( 1 \) is \( 1 \) itself, which contradicts the fact that \( p \) is a prime number, as primes are greater than \( 1 \).

Therefore, our initial assumption must be false, and it follows that \( p > n \).

Hence, for every natural number \( n \), there exists a prime number \( p \) such that \( p > n \), demonstrating that there are infinitely many prime numbers.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: If φ implies ψ, then substituting any term s into both φ and ψ maintains the implication φ → ψ.
informal_proof: Assume that φ implies ψ. When we substitute a term s into both φ and ψ, we obtain φ[s] and ψ[s]. Since substitution is a syntactic operation that replaces terms within the logical expressions, the implication is preserved. If φ → ψ is true, and both φ and ψ are substituted with φ[s] and ψ[s] respectively, then φ[s] implies ψ[s] must also hold. This is because substitution maintains the logical structure of the implication, ensuring that if φ implies ψ before substitution, their substituted versions φ[s] and ψ[s] preserve this implication. The result follows directly from the properties of substitution and implication in formal logic.

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : Repr (Formula α) := ⟨fun t _ => toStr t⟩
instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: Substitution distributes over disjunction, meaning that substituting a term for a variable in a disjunction of two formulas results in the disjunction of the substituted formulas.
informal_proof: Substitution, by its definition in formal logic, applies separately to each disjunct in a disjunction. Therefore, substituting a term \( s \) for a variable in a disjunction \( \varphi \lor \psi \) is equivalent to substituting \( s \) into each individual formula \( \varphi \) and \( \psi \) and then forming the disjunction of the substituted formulas. This preservation of structure under substitution confirms the distributivity of substitution over disjunction.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: Substituting a term into a conjunction of two propositions is equivalent to substituting the term into each proposition separately and then forming their conjunction.
informal_proof:
To see why this is true, consider that substitution operates uniformly across logical connectives. When applied to a conjunction (φ ∧ ψ), substitution replaces the relevant term in both φ and ψ. Since the conjunction of the substituted terms maintains the logical structure of the original conjunction, it follows that substituting into the conjunction (φ ∧ ψ).subst s results in (φ.subst s). 
Similarly, substituting separately into each component (φ.subst s ∧ ψ.subst s) preserves the relation due to the definition of substitution in propositional logic. Since both operations yield equivalent results, we have the equality by definition. Therefore, the substitution into the conjunction equals the conjunction of substitutions.

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : Repr (Formula α) := ⟨fun t _ => toStr t⟩
instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : Repr (Formula α) := ⟨fun t _ => toStr t⟩
instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

end ToString

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: The `subst` function takes a substitution function `s` and a well-formed formula (wff) and substitutes each occurrence of an atomic proposition in the formula with the corresponding proposition given by `s`. This substitution is uniformly applied across all parts of the formula, preserving the logical connectives and structure.
informal_proof:
To formally establish that the `subst` function behaves as described, we will use an inductive proof based on the structure of well-formed formulas (wff). We will consider each case of the formula's construction and verify that `subst` applies the substitution uniformly.

1. **Base Case (Atomic Propositions):**  
   For an atomic proposition `a`, by definition:
   ```
   subst s (Atom a) = s a
   ```
   This directly replaces the atomic proposition `a` with `s a`, as required.

2. **Negation Case:**  
   For a formula `∼φ`, the substitution is:
   ```
   subst s (∼φ) = ∼(φ.subst s)
   ```
   Here, `subst` applies to `φ`, and then the negation is applied outside. This maintains the logical structure.

3. **Implication Case:**  
   For an implication `φ → ψ`, substitution yields:
   ```
   subst s (φ → ψ) = (φ.subst s) → (ψ.subst s)
   ```
   Substitution is applied to both `φ` and `ψ`, preserving the implication structure.

4. **Conjunction and Disjunction Cases:**  
   For conjunction `φ ⋏ ψ` and disjunction `φ ⋎ ψ`, substitutions are:
   ```
   subst s (φ ⋏ ψ) = (φ.subst s) ⋏ (ψ.subst s)
   ```
   ```
   subst s (φ ⋎ ψ) = (φ.subst s) ⋎ (ψ.subst s)
   ```
   Again, substitution is uniformly applied to both operands, preserving the logical connectives.

5. **Inductive Step:**  
   Since all wffs can be constructed inductively from atomic propositions using these logical connectives, the uniform application of `subst` ensures that every atomic proposition in the formula is replaced by its corresponding proposition in `s`, while the structure of the formula remains intact.

By induction, we conclude that the `subst` function uniformly replaces each atomic proposition in any wff with its corresponding proposition under `s`, preserving the formula's logical structure and connectives.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

theorem nat_iff {f : α → β → σ} : Primrec₂ f ↔ Nat.Primrec
    (.unpaired fun m n => encode <| (@decode α _ m).bind fun a => (@decode β _ n).map (f a)) := by
  have :
    ∀ (a : Option α) (b : Option β),
      Option.map (fun p : α × β => f p.1 p.2)
          (Option.bind a fun a : α => Option.map (Prod.mk a) b) =
        Option.bind a fun a => Option.map (f a) b := fun a b => by
          cases a <;> cases b <;> rfl
  simp [Primrec₂, Primrec, this]

informal_statement: The encoding and decoding functions 'toNat' and 'ofNat' are inverses of each other. That is, for any formula φ in the metalanguage, applying 'toNat' followed by 'ofNat' returns the original formula φ.
informal_proof: Consider an arbitrary formula φ in the metalanguage. The function 'toNat' encodes φ into a natural number representation, while 'ofNat' decodes natural numbers back into their corresponding formulas. The proof for each case is based on simplifying the definitions and ensuring that the decoding process accurately reconstructs the original formula. For atomic formulas, 'ofNat' correctly extracts the original code. For logical connectives like negation (¬), disjunction (∨), conjuction (∧), and implication (→), 'ofNat' reversely decodes each logical operation to match the original formula. Since all cases are handled correctly, 'ofNat (toNat φ)' reconstructs φ exactly, proving that the encoding and decoding are inverses.

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : Repr (Formula α) := ⟨fun t _ => toStr t⟩
instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

end ToString

@[simp] lemma and_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋏ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋏ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Wedge.wedge]
@[simp] lemma or_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋎ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋎ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Vee.vee]
@[simp] lemma imp_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ➝ φ₂ = ψ₁ ➝ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Arrow.arrow]
@[simp] lemma neg_inj (φ ψ : Formula α) : ∼φ = ∼ψ ↔ φ = ψ := by simp[Tilde.tilde]

-- lemma neg_def (φ : Formula α) : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥ := rfl

lemma iff_def (φ ψ : Formula α) : φ ⭤ ψ = (φ ➝ ψ) ⋏ (ψ ➝ φ) := by rfl

def complexity : Formula α → ℕ
| atom _  => 0
| ⊤       => 0
| ⊥       => 0
| ∼φ      => φ.complexity + 1
| φ ➝ ψ  => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋏ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋎ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1

@[simp] lemma complexity_bot : complexity (⊥ : Formula α) = 0 := rfl
@[simp] lemma complexity_top : complexity (⊤ : Formula α) = 0 := rfl
annotation: @[simp] lemma complexity_top : complexity (⊤ : Formula α) = 0 := rfl

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: The `ofNat` function assigns a specific formula from the `Formula α` type to each natural number. For the number `0`, it assigns `none`, and for numbers greater than `0`, it constructs formulas based on an index and a character, using predefined operations such as negation, implication, conjunction, and disjunction to form complex logical expressions.
informal_proof:
To understand how the `ofNat` function operates, we can break it down step by step:

1. **Base Case (0):**  
   For the natural number `0`, the function directly returns `none`, indicating the simplest case.

2. **Successor Case (1):**  
   For any number greater than `0`, it decomposes the index into `0` and handles it by mapping the formula atom from the character. This assigns fundamental logical atoms at the base level of the formula hierarchy.

3. **Logical Constants:**  
   When the index is `1`, it assigns `⊤` (truth) and `⊥` (falsity), providing the foundational logical constants necessary for subsequent formula construction.

4. **Negation Operation (3):**  
   For higher indices, the function constructs negated formulas by checking if the character's value remains less than the current number and negating the corresponding formula.

5. **Implication Operation (4):**  
   It also constructs formulas involving implication by combining logical expressions in a directed manner.

6. **Conjunction Operation (5):**  
   For further complexity, the function employs conjunction (logical "and") when the index leads to a relatively simple combination of previously defined formulas.

7. **Disjunction Operation (6):**  
   Finally, it introduces disjunction (logical "or") for more intricate logical expressions, allowing the function to build upon the base case through these operations.

Through this structured approach, every natural number is systematically assigned a unique and appropriately complex formula within the `Formula α` type, ensuring a comprehensive and inductive construction of logical expressions.

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : Repr (Formula α) := ⟨fun t _ => toStr t⟩
instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

end ToString

@[simp] lemma and_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋏ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋏ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Wedge.wedge]
@[simp] lemma or_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ⋎ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋎ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Vee.vee]
@[simp] lemma imp_inj (φ₁ ψ₁ φ₂ ψ₂ : Formula α) : φ₁ ➝ φ₂ = ψ₁ ➝ ψ₂ ↔ φ₁ = ψ₁ ∧ φ₂ = ψ₂ := by simp[Arrow.arrow]
@[simp] lemma neg_inj (φ ψ : Formula α) : ∼φ = ∼ψ ↔ φ = ψ := by simp[Tilde.tilde]

-- lemma neg_def (φ : Formula α) : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥ := rfl

lemma iff_def (φ ψ : Formula α) : φ ⭤ ψ = (φ ➝ ψ) ⋏ (ψ ➝ φ) := by rfl

def complexity : Formula α → ℕ
| atom _  => 0
| ⊤       => 0
| ⊥       => 0
| ∼φ      => φ.complexity + 1
| φ ➝ ψ  => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋏ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1
| φ ⋎ ψ   => max φ.complexity ψ.complexity + 1

@[simp] lemma complexity_bot : complexity (⊥ : Formula α) = 0 := by exact?

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
C1_dependencies.compilationAlias:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

theorem of_prim {n f} : Primrec f → @Primrec' n f :=
  suffices ∀ f, Nat.Primrec f → @Primrec' 1 fun v => f v.head from fun hf =>
    (pred.comp₁ _ <|
          (this _ hf).comp₁ (fun m => Encodable.encode <| (@decode (List.Vector ℕ n) _ m).map f)
            Primrec'.encode).of_eq
      fun i => by simp [encodek]
  fun f hf => by
  induction hf with
  | zero => exact const 0
  | succ => exact succ
  | left => exact unpair₁ head
  | right => exact unpair₂ head
  | pair _ _ hf hg => exact natPair.comp₂ _ hf hg
  | comp _ _ hf hg => exact hf.comp₁ _ hg
  | prec _ _ hf hg =>
    simpa using
      prec' (unpair₂ head) (hf.comp₁ _ (unpair₁ head))
        (hg.comp₁ _ <|
          natPair.comp₂ _ (unpair₁ <| tail <| tail head) (natPair.comp₂ _ head (tail head)))

- The constants `⊤` and `⊥` are mapped to specific numbers.
- Negation, implication, conjunction, disjunction, etc., areEach assigned a unique pair, which is then combined into a natural number using a function. This ensures that each distinct formula receives a distinct natural number. The exact encoding ensures that the function is systematic and unique for each formula type.

  | atom   : α → Formula α

  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

instance : ToString (Formula α) := ⟨toStr⟩

informal_statement: For any property `C` defined over formulas, the inductive definition of `C` via `rec'` accurately captures all cases of well-formed formulas constructed using implication, conjunction, disjunction, and atomic formulas, along with the base cases for falsity and truth.
informal_proof:
We aim to show that for any property `C` defined over formulas, the inductive definition provided by `rec'` correctly associates each formula with its corresponding property `C`. This proof is constructed using structural induction on the formulas.

1. **Base Cases:**
   - **Atomic Formula (`atom a`):** By definition, `C (atom a)` holds according to `hatom`.
   - **Falsity (`⊥`):** `C (⊥)` is satisfied by `hfalsum`.
   - **Truth (`⊤`):** `C (⊤)` is satisfied by `hverum`.

2. **Inductive Step:**
   - **Negation (`¬φ`):** Assuming `C φ` holds, `C (¬φ)` holds by invoking `hneg`.
   - **Implication (`φ → ψ`):** Assuming `C φ` and `C ψ` hold, `C (φ → ψ)` holds by applying `himp`.
   - **Conjunction (`φ ∧ ψ`):** Assuming `C φ` and `C ψ` hold, `C (φ ∧ ψ)` holds by using `hand`.
   - **Disjunction (`φ ∨ ψ`):** Assuming `C φ` and `C ψ` hold, `C (φ ∨ ψ)` holds by employing `hor`.

By systematically applying these rules, we ensure that all formula structures are accounted for, and thus `rec'` correctly defines `C` for every possible formula.

informal_statement: There exists a systematic method for defining classes over well-formed formulas (wffs) in logic by recursively examining their structure and breaking them down into atomic components and logical connectives.
informal_proof:
To establish this method, we define a function or predicate `C` over formulas using structural induction. The definition proceeds by examining each type of formula:

1. **Atomic Formulas**: For an atomic formula `atom a`, `C` is defined directly by the clause `hatom`.
2. **Negation**: For a negated formula `∼φ`, `C` is defined by the clause `hneg`.
3. **Implication**: For an implication formula `φ ➝ ψ`, `C` is defined by the clause `himp`.
4. **Conjunction**: For a conjunction formula `φ ⋏ ψ`, `C` is defined by the clause `hand`.
5. **Disjunction**: For a disjunction formula `φ ⋎ ψ`, `C` is defined by the clause `hor`.

By verifying each clause, we ensure that `C` correctly applies to all formula types. This step-by-step verification aligns with natural language reasoning, demonstrating that any formula can be classified by systematically examining its constituent parts.

informal_statement: The complexity of the logical OR of two formulas is equal to the maximum complexity of the individual formulas plus one.
informal_proof:
To determine the complexity of the logical OR of two formulas, we consider the maximum complexity among the individual formulas and add one. This increment accounts for the OR operation itself introducing an additional layer of complexity.

For the first part of the proof, we start by noting that the complexity of any formula is determined by its structure, specifically the nesting of logical operations. The logical OR operation combines two formulas into one, effectively adding a layer of nesting.

Given two formulas, φ and ψ, their combined formula φ ∨ ψ introduces an additional layer of complexity. To calculate the complexity of φ ∨ ψ, we first determine the complexities of φ and ψ individually, which are denoted as complexity(φ) and complexity(ψ), respectively.

The maximum of these two complexities, max(complexity(φ), complexity(ψ)), represents the depth of the deeper nesting within either formula. When we combine these formulas with an OR operation, the resulting formula's complexity increases by one, reflecting the addition of the OR operation.

This additional layer is accounted for by adding 1 to the maximum of the individual complexities. Therefore, the complexity of φ ∨ ψ is precisely max(complexity(φ), complexity(ψ)) + 1.

This reasoning shows that the complexity of a logical OR operation between two formulas is indeed equal to the maximum complexity of the individual formulas plus one.

informal_statement: The complexity of the disjunction of two logical formulas is equal to the maximum complexity of the individual formulas plus one.
informal_proof:
To establish that the complexity of the disjunction \( \varphi \lor \psi \) is equal to the maximum complexity of the individual formulas plus one, we proceed as follows:

1. **Base Case**: Consider the simplest case where both \( \varphi \) and \( \psi \) have a complexity of zero (i.e., they are atomic propositions). Then, \( \max(\varphi.complexity, \psi.complexity) + 1 = \max(0, 0) + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1 \). Thus, the complexity of \( \varphi \lor \psi \) is indeed 1, which aligns with the definition.

2. **Inductive Step**: Assume the property holds for all formulas with complexity less than or equal to \( n \). Now, consider formulas \( \varphi \) and \( \psi \) each of complexity \( n + 1 \). Since the disjunction \( \varphi \lor \psi \) is a combination of two formulas of complexity \( n + 1 \), its complexity should be \( n + 1 + 1 = n + 2 \).

3. **Recursive Definition Application**: By the definition of the `complexity` function in Lean4, \( complexity(\varphi \lor \psi) = \max(\varphi.complexity, \psi.complexity) + 1 \). Given our inductive hypothesis, substituting \( \varphi.complexity \) and \( \psi.complexity \) with \( n + 1 \) confirms that \( complexity(\varphi \lor \psi) = (n + 1) + 1 = n + 2 \).

4. **Conclusion**: Therefore, by induction, the complexity of the disjunction \( \varphi \lor \psi \) is always one greater than the maximum complexity of \( \varphi \) and \( \psi \), confirming the statement.

This completes the proof.

2. **Logical AND Operation**: The logical AND operation combines two formulas. In logic, the AND of two formulas \( \phi \) and \( \psi \) is denoted as \( \phi \land \psi \).

3. **Combining Formulas**: When we form the AND of two formulas, we are essentially creating a new, more complex formula that depends on both original formulas. This dependency introduces an additional layer of complexity.

4. **Calculating Complexity for AND**: If \( \phi \) has a complexity of \( n \) and \( \psi \) has a complexity of \( m \), then the formula \( \phi \land \psi \) introduces a new layer that depends on both \( \phi \) and \( \psi \). rag.content:
theorem nat_findGreatest {f : α → ℕ} {p : α → ℕ → Prop} [∀ x n, Decidable (p x n)]
    (hf : Primrec f) (hp : PrimrecRel p) : Primrec fun x => (f x).findGreatest (p x) :=
  (nat_rec' (h := fun x nih => if p x (nih.1 + 1) then nih.1 + 1 else nih.2)
    hf (const 0) (ite (hp.comp fst (snd |> fst.comp |> succ.comp))
      (snd |> fst.comp |> succ.comp) (snd.comp snd))).of_eq fun x => by
        induction f x <;> simp [Nat.findGreatest, *]

informal_statement: For any two logical formulas φ and ψ, the complexity of their conjunction (φ ∧ ψ) is equal to the maximum complexity of φ and ψ, plus one.
informal_proof:
First, we consider two arbitrary logical formulas, φ and ψ. 

We then note that the complexity of their conjunction, φ ∧ ψ, is defined as one more than the maximum complexity between φ and ψ. This means that combining two formulas with a logical 'and' adds an additional layer of complexity to the resulting formula.

To prove this, we introduce φ and ψ as arbitrary formulas. Next, we split the goal of proving the complexity of φ ∧ ψ into two separate goals using the constructor tactic. This tactic addresses both sides of the conjunction independently.

For each side, we assume the hypothesis that the conjunction φ ∧ ψ holds, which implies that both φ and ψ hold individually. By examining each side, we determine the complexity of each formula and then combine them, adding one to the maximum complexity to account for the logical 'and' operation.

Thus, we have shown that the complexity of the conjunction φ ∧ ψ is indeed equal to the maximum complexity of φ and ψ, plus one.

To establish that the complexity of the implication of two formulas φ and ψ is equal to the maximum of their individual complexities plus one, we can analyze the definition of complexity provided in the `simp` lemma.

Given the definition of complexity in this context:
- The complexity of a formula φ is measured as a natural number.
- The complexity of the implication `imp φ ψ` is specifically defined as the maximum of the complexities of φ and ψ, incremented by one.

This definition ensures that the complexity of an implication is directly tied to the complexities of its constituent formulas. By adding the implication operator (`imp`), we introduce an additional layer of complexity, which is reflected in the "+1" component of the definition.

Thus, by the very definition provided, we can conclude that the complexity of `imp φ ψ` is indeed the maximum of the complexities of φ and ψ plus one, aligning perfectly with the statement.

import Foundation.Logic.LogicSymbol
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic

namespace LO.IntProp

inductive Formula (α : Type u) : Type u
  | atom   : α → Formula α
  | verum  : Formula α
  | falsum : Formula α
  | neg    : Formula α → Formula α
  | and    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | or     : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  | imp    : Formula α → Formula α → Formula α
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Formula

instance : LogicalConnective (Formula α) where
  tilde := neg
  arrow := imp
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  bot := falsum

section ToString

variable [ToString α]

def toStr : Formula α → String
  | ⊤       => "\\top"
  | ⊥       => "\\bot"
  | atom a  => "{" ++ toString a ++ "}"
  | ∼φ      => "\\lnot " ++ toStr φ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | φ ➝ ψ   => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\rightarrow " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"

rag.content:
theorem nat_findGreatest {f : α → ℕ} {p : α → ℕ → Prop} [∀ x n, Decidable (p x n)]
    (hf : Primrec f) (hp : PrimrecRel p) : Primrec fun x => (f x).findGreatest (p x) :=
  (nat_rec' (h := fun x nih => if p x (nih.1 + 1) then nih.1 + 1 else nih.2)
    hf (const 0) (ite (hp.comp fst (snd |> fst.comp |> succ.comp))
      (snd |> fst.comp |> succ.comp) (snd.comp snd))).of_eq fun x => by
        induction f x <;> simp [Nat.findGreatest, *]

informal_statement: The complexity of an implication $(φ \rightarrow ψ)$ in propositional logic is defined as the maximum of the complexities of the antecedent $φ$ and the consequent $ψ$, incremented by one. That is, $complexity(φ \rightarrow ψ) = \max\{complexity(φ), complexity(ψ)\} + 1$.
informal_proof:
To establish that the complexity of an implication $(φ \rightarrow ψ)$ is given by $\max\{complexity(φ), complexity(ψ)\} + 1$, we proceed based on the definition of the $complexity$ function.

1. **Definition of Complexity**: The $complexity$ function is defined inductively:
   - For a propositional variable, $complexity(v) = 0$.
   - For a compound formula $φ \circ ψ$, where $\circ$ represents a logical connective (such as $\land$, $\lor$, or $\rightarrow$), the complexity is defined as the maximum of the complexities of its components plus one: $complexity(φ \circ ψ) = \max\{complexity(φ), complexity(ψ)\} + 1$.

2. **Applying the Definition to Implication**: Consider the implication formula $φ \rightarrow ψ$. By the definition of the $complexity$ function:
   - $complexity(φ \rightarrow ψ) = \max\{complexity(φ), complexity(ψ)\} + 1$.

3. **Justification of the Formula**:
   - The implication $φ \rightarrow ψ$ introduces an additional layer of complexity beyond the more complex of its antecedent $φ$ and consequent $ψ$. This additional layer accounts for the logical operation of implication itself, necessitating an increase in complexity by one.

Therefore, the complexity of the implication $(φ \rightarrow ψ)$ is indeed $\max\{complexity(φ), complexity(ψ)\} + 1$, as per the inductive definition of the $complexity$ function.

informal_statement: For any natural number \( n \), \( 0 \) is less than or equal to \( n \).
informal_proof:
First, we consider the base case where \( n = 0 \). By definition, \( 0 \leq 0 \) holds true.

Next, for the inductive step, assume that \( n = m + 1 \) for some natural number \( m \). Given the inductive hypothesis that \( 0 \leq m \), adding \( 1 \) to both sides gives \( 1 \leq m + 1 \). Therefore, \( 0 \leq n \) holds for \( n = m + 1 \).

By induction, \( 0 \leq n \) is true for all natural numbers \( n \).

informal_statement: The complexity of a logical formula is defined recursively. Atomic formulas and constants, such as true (⊤) and false (⊥), have a complexity of 0. The complexity of a negated formula (∼φ) is the complexity of φ plus 1. For logical connectives such as implication (φ → ψ), conjunction (φ ∧ ψ), and disjunction (φ ∨ ψ), the complexity is the maximum of the complexities of the two formulas involved, plus 1.

informal_statement: For any two formulas φ and ψ, the statement "φ if and only if ψ" is logically equivalent to the conjunction of "φ implies ψ" and "ψ implies φ."
informal_proof: The biconditional statement "φ if and only if ψ" means that φ and ψ imply each other. Therefore, by definition, it is equivalent to having both "φ implies ψ" and "ψ implies φ." This captures the essence of logical equivalence, where each formula's truth value mirrors the other's.

informal_statement: If the disjunction of two formulas \( \phi_1 \) or \( \phi_2 \) is logically equivalent to the disjunction of another two formulas \( \psi_1 \) or \( \psi_2 \), then \( \phi_1 \) is logically equivalent to \( \psi_1 \) and \( \phi_2 \) is logically equivalent to \( \psi_2 \).
informal_proof:
Assume that \( \phi_1 \lor \phi_2 \) is logically equivalent to \( \psi_1 \lor \psi_2 \).

By the definition of logical equivalence, \( \phi_1 \lor \phi_2 \) and \( \psi_1 \lor \psi_2 \) have the same truth value in all possible interpretations. Since a disjunction is true if at least one of the disjuncts is true, and false otherwise, the only way for two disjunctions to have the same truth value in all cases is if each corresponding disjunct is equivalent.

Therefore, \( \phi_1 \) must be equivalent to \( \psi_1 \) and \( \phi_2 \) must be equivalent to \( \psi_2 \).

informal_statement: If the conjunction of two propositions φ₁ and φ₂ is equal to the conjunction of two other propositions ψ₁ and ψ₂ in a Heyting algebra, then φ₁ must be equal to ψ₁ and φ₂ must be equal to ψ₂.
informal_proof: Assume φ₁ ∧ φ₂ equals ψ₁ ∧ ψ₂ in the Heyting algebra. By the definition of conjunction in a Heyting algebra, if φ₁ ∧ φ₂ equals ψ₁ ∧ ψ₂, then both φ₁ must be equal to ψ₁ and φ₂ must be equal to ψ₂ individually. This follows from the properties of conjunction, which in a Heyting algebra, allow us to simplify the conjunctions step by step. Hence, we conclude that φ₁ = ψ₁ and φ₂ = ψ₂.

informal_statement: The `toStr` function converts a Lean4 logical formula into a LaTeX string, handling logical connectives with proper formatting and escaping.
informal_proof:
First, we consider the base cases of the formula structure in Lean4:
1. If the formula is `⊤` (true), the function returns `\\top`.
2. If the formula is `⊥` (false), the function returns `\\bot`.

Next, for an atomic formula `atom a`, the function wraps its string representation in curly braces, resulting in `{ a }`.

For logical connectives:
3. The negation `∼φ` is converted to `\\lnot {φ}`, ensuring proper escaping.
4. The conjunction `φ ⋏ ψ` is converted to `\\left(\\lnot {φ} \\land {ψ} \\right)`, with logical connectives wrapped in parentheses.
5. The disjunction `φ ⋎ ψ` is converted to `\\left(\\lnot {φ} \\lor {ψ} \\right)`.
6. The implication `φ ➝ ψ` is converted to `\\left(\\lnot {φ} \\rightarrow {ψ} \\right)`.

By handling each case explicitly, the function ensures that logical formulas are accurately represented in LaTeX with appropriate formatting and escaping, making them readable and properly structured. This guarantees that any formula passed through `toStr` will produce a correctly formatted LaTeX string as per the defined rules.

<STATEMENT>

For any propositions \( a \) and \( b \), the logical conjunction \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \).

</STATEMENT>

<PROOF>

First, we consider two arbitrary propositions \( a \) and \( b \). The logical conjunction \( a \land b \) asserts that both \( a \) and \( b \) are true. Since the order of the conjuncts does not affect the truth value, asserting \( b \land a \) also requires both \( b \) and \( a \) to be true. Therefore, \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \). This demonstrates the commutative property of logical conjunction.

instance (priority := 100) toSubtractionMonoid : SubtractionMonoid α where
  neg_neg a := by
    by_cases h : a = ⊤
    · simp [h]
    · have h2 : ¬ -a = ⊤ := fun nh ↦ h <| neg_eq_top.mp nh
      replace h2 : a + (-a + - -a) = a + 0 := congrArg (a + ·) (add_neg_cancel_of_ne_top h2)
      rw [← add_assoc, add_neg_cancel_of_ne_top h] at h2
      simp only [zero_add, add_zero] at h2
      exact h2
  neg_add_rev a b := by
    by_cases ha : a = ⊤
    · simp [ha]
    by_cases hb : b = ⊤
    · simp [hb]
    apply (_ : Function.Injective (a + b + ·))
    · dsimp
      rw [add_neg_cancel_of_ne_top, ← add_assoc, add_assoc a,
        add_neg_cancel_of_ne_top hb, add_zero,
        add_neg_cancel_of_ne_top ha]
      simp [ha, hb]
    · apply Function.LeftInverse.injective (g := (-(a + b) + ·))
      intro x
      dsimp only
      rw [← add_assoc, add_comm (-(a + b)), add_neg_cancel_of_ne_top, zero_add]
      simp [ha, hb]
  neg_eq_of_add a b h := by
    have oh := congrArg (-a + ·) h
    dsimp only at oh
    rw [add_zero, ← add_assoc, add_comm (-a), add_neg_cancel_of_ne_top, zero_add] at oh
    · exact oh.symm
    intro v
    simp [v] at h

informal_statement: Falsum is a formula that represents a contradiction, always taking the value false.
informal_proof: Falsum, denoted as ⊥, is a constant in the Formula α type that represents a proposition that is always false. This is a fundamental concept in logic, often referred to as an absolute falsehood. In Intuitionistic Logic, which Lean4's formal system is based on, falsum serves as a crucial building block for defining logical connectives and proving theorems. Its presence in the Formula α type underscores its role as a basic, irrefutable contradiction within the logical framework. Therefore, by definition, falsum is a formula that is always false, as it has no models in any interpretation—i.e., there are no truth-value assignments under which it evaluates to true.

informal_statement: For all propositions \( a \) and \( b \), \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \).
informal_proof:
To establish that \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \) for all propositions \( a \) and \( b \), we need to demonstrate the commutative property of the logical "and" operation.

**Forward Direction (\( a \land b \) implies \( b \land a \)):**

Assume \( a \land b \) is true. By the definition of logical "and", this means both \( a \) and \( b \) are true individually. Since both \( a \) and \( b \) hold, it follows directly that \( b \) and \( a \) are also both true. Therefore, \( b \land a \) is true.

**Reverse Direction (\( b \land a \) implies \( a \land b \)):**

Conversely, assume \( b \land a \) is true. Again, by the definition of logical "and", both \( b \) and \( a \) are true. Since both \( b \) and \( a \) hold, it follows that \( a \) and \( b \) are both true as well. Therefore, \( a \land b \) is true.

Since we've shown both directions, we conclude that \( a \land b \) is equivalent to \( b \land a \).
